title: Oscar and the Harbor
premise: Silas Amberdale built a career orchestrating other people's perfect days after his own engagement collapsed, and he has sworn off love ever since. When a dying client's will leaves the Harbor Orchard jointly to Silas and to Wren Calloway — the woman who walked out on him a decade ago — the two are legally bound to restore the orchard together within one year or lose it to a developer. As seasons turn over the neglected trees, old wounds reopen into something tenderer, forcing Silas to choose between the flawless reputation he hid behind and a future with Wren that can't be scripted. In the end, they harvest the orchard's first crop together, sign nothing away, and marry quietly among the trees — not as a production, but as a promise.
about_author: Yara Pemberton is a former estate lawyer turned novelist who writes about inheritance, salt air, and second chances from a converted boathouse in Maine. Her debut, 'Oscar and the Harbor,' was inspired by an orchard deed she once probated with two names she never forgot.

chapters.title: The Deed That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: POV Silas. A meticulous wedding at a coastal estate goes flawlessly, yet Silas feels nothing, and afterward his lawyer delivers shocking news: a late client left him half of the derelict Harbor Orchard. The other half belongs to Wren Calloway, the fiancée who left him ten years ago. Beat: numb competence cracked open by the past arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Tree
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren, a struggling arborist in another city, receives the same letter and drives to the orchard intending to sell her share immediately. She finds Silas already there, measuring the land for a buyout. Their first meeting is brittle, professional, and charged. Beat: guarded hostility masking grief neither has finished mourning.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: POV Silas. The will's strange condition surfaces: joint restoration for one year, or the developer Marcus Vane acquires everything. Silas proposes buying Wren out; she refuses, needing the orchard's income. They sign an uneasy co-tenancy agreement. Beat: reluctant alliance formed out of necessity, each convinced the other will blink first.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Winter work begins. Wren teaches Silas to prune while he catalogs the orchard like an event venue, and their rhythms slowly braid together. A shared flask of cider and one honest argument about who ended what crack the ice. Beat: grudging respect blooming alongside the first bare buds.

chapters.title: Vane Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Developer Marcus Vane arrives with a generous buyout and veiled threats, revealing he engineered the will's deadline through a loan against the estate. Silas, tempted by the escape, hides the offer from Wren. Beat: corruption of power introduced — money whispering that the easy exit is also the moral failure.

chapters.title: Blossom and Betrayal
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Spring blossoms arrive, and so does Wren's discovery of Silas's secret meetings with Vane. Feeling history repeat — Silas choosing ambition over honesty — she walks the rows alone at night. He finds her and confesses everything, including his fear that he only ruins what he loves. Beat: rupture before bloom; raw vulnerability offered.

chapters.title: The Found Family
chapters.summary: POV alternating. The orchard's odd caretakers — retired ferryman Oscar, teenage runaway Junie, and Wren's estranged aunt — rally around the failing project, becoming the family neither lead ever had. Together they plan a harvest festival to prove the orchard's viability to the bank. Beat: found family as the antidote to inherited wounds.

chapters.title: What Money Can't Graft
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Vane escalates: he buys the orchard's water rights and offers Silas full ownership if he betrays the co-tenancy. At the same moment, Wren asks Silas directly whether he wants her or the escape. Standing under the oldest tree, Silas tears up Vane's contract. Beat: climax of choice — power refused, love chosen aloud.

chapters.title: Harvest Eve
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Vane's lawyers move to void the will, but Oscar produces evidence the loan was predatory, and the community floods the hearing in support. The deadline dissolves; the orchard is theirs free and clear. Exhausted, Wren and Silas admit, finally and plainly, that they never stopped loving each other. Beat: external victory and internal surrender arriving together.

chapters.title: A Wedding Without a Planner
chapters.summary: POV Silas. One year later, the orchard heavy with fruit, Silas and Wren marry beneath the oldest tree — no seating charts, no production, just Junie playing fiddle and Oscar giving away the bride. Silas plans weddings again, but now he believes in them. Beat: resolution — inheritance reclaimed as legacy, love moved back into present tense.
